claims.text: Separately modeling lattice and electronic heat transport will improve prediction accuracy for HfNbTaTiZr relative to prior analytical models that conflate the two channels.
The new approach will predict the individual thermal-conductivity contributions within ±15% of experimental values.
Samples containing less than 0.1 wt% oxygen can be treated as eliminating extrinsic oxygen effects.
A sample containing 1 wt% oxygen represents a reported experimental condition for HfNbTaTiZr.
The proposed model will calculate phonon and electronic contributions separately using DFT-derived scattering information and temperature-dependent analytical phonon-transport models.
Below 200 K, lattice and electronic thermal-conductivity contributions in HfNbTaTiZr are of comparable magnitude.
Above 300 K, lattice heat transport is expected to dominate, particularly in low-oxygen HfNbTaTiZr.
Assuming a perfect, defect-free single crystal with controlled trace oxygen permits electron and phonon scattering mechanisms to be decoupled.
Independent evaluation of electron and phonon scattering avoids conflation of the two heat-transport channels.
Incorporating force-constant variations and temperature effects captures temperature-dependent transport phenomena in more detail than previous methods.
Above 300 K, lattice thermal conductivity in low-oxygen HfNbTaTiZr will be at least twice the electronic contribution.
The predicted total thermal conductivity will remain within ±15% of experimental measurements over the applicable range.
Below 200 K, the model will reproduce near-equality between lattice and electronic thermal-conductivity contributions.
Existing single-parameter analytical estimates deviate from measurements by 30–50%.
Existing single-parameter approaches do not discriminate between lattice and electronic heat transport.
The hypothesis applies to bulk, defect-free crystalline HfNbTaTiZr between approximately 100 and 1200 K with controlled oxygen content up to 1 wt%.
The approach may not apply to specimens with significant extrinsic defects or oxygen contamination above 1 wt%.
Microstructural defects, oxygen variation, and temperature-dependent electron–phonon interactions may impair separation of the two transport channels.
Laser-flash and thermoelectric measurements can independently determine lattice and electronic thermal-conductivity contributions across 100–1200 K.
A deviation greater than ±15% at any temperature, or failure of the predicted high-temperature lattice-to-electronic ratio, would falsify the hypothesis.

contradictions.description: The material is repeatedly described as perfect and defect-free while also containing controlled oxygen impurities, including 1 wt% oxygen. Unless oxygen is an intended constituent on specified lattice sites, this is in tension with the perfect defect-free assumption.

The main hypothesis appears to require individual lattice and electronic contributions to be within ±15% of experiment, whereas the predicted outcome explicitly applies the ±15% requirement to total conductivity; the accuracy target is therefore internally ambiguous.
